A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work. Their main text, equations, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching content moved or renumbered in v3.

before.justification: v2 reports original Monte Carlo simulations of ST, Lasso, and ridge regression, including stability, distributional behavior, and confidence-interval coverage in Figures 1–5.

after.justification: v3 retains those original simulations and adds an empirical coverage-and-width comparison of confidence intervals in Figure 6.

M1.justification: The estimators, loss functions, relative-stability definition, and confidence-interval construction in Proposition 6.1 are unchanged. Figure 6 evaluates an existing construction rather than introducing a method.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate single algorithms and model comparisons using the same sparse and dense Gaussian linear-regression settings. Figure 6 reuses the sparse ST setting of Figure 2.

E2.justification: Figure 6 newly evaluates the Proposition 6.1 interval against the CV CLT interval. Proposition 6.1 was already presented in v2 but did not participate in a reported empirical comparison.

E3.justification: The added Figure 6 comparison measures coverage and interval width across sample sizes at nominal 95% coverage. The retained experiments keep their data generation, folds, sample sizes, and penalty-selection procedures.

E4.justification: Figure 6 adds a supplementary analysis of the coverage-versus-width tradeoff of Proposition 6.1. The existing ridge and dense-ST analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report the same 50,000 distributional replications, 5,000,000 or 1,000,000 stability-estimation replications, seed practice, and Monte Carlo uncertainty calculations. Figure 6 evaluates existing interval rules without introducing a new uncertainty-reporting procedure.

E6.justification: Figure 6 newly reports approximately 83–85% coverage for the CV CLT interval versus approximately 100% for Proposition 6.1 at a 95% target, with the latter several orders of magnitude wider. Reported values and findings in Figures 1–5 are unchanged.

T1.justification: v3 explicitly adds p <= n to the linear-model setup and states the resulting almost-sure invertibility of X-transpose-X. The main theorems and proofs are retained; Lemma 4.1 matches v2's Lemma H.2, whose proof is relocated rather than newly supplied.

C1.justification: The central claims remain that individually stable ST and Lasso fits can yield relatively unstable comparisons and invalid CV inference. The rewritten introduction retains this contribution and its scope.

C2.justification: Both versions retain the same distribution/model limitations, stable counterexamples, and open question about whether relative instability always implies CV invalidity. The explanation that ignored positive correlations can make Proposition 6.1 conservative was already present; Figure 6 adds supporting evidence.

D1.justification: The experimental setup appendix, moved from L to M, retains the same software, adaptive inner-CV search, reproducibility information, and code-access statement. No additional implementation or resource details accompany Figure 6.

R1.justification: v3 adds Eaton (2007), removes Mukherjee et al. (2006), and expands discussion of the already-cited Bates et al. (2024), distinguishing its single-algorithm expected-error coverage findings from this paper's model-comparison failures.

P1.justification: v3 revises the introduction and parts of the preliminary and CV exposition, promotes an appendix lemma into Section 4, reorganizes its proof placement, and updates the publication header. The overall section sequence and most text remain intact.

P2.justification: v3 adds the two-panel Figure 6, adds single/comparison loss notation to panel labels in Figures 2–5, and relocates Figures 4–5 within the appendix layout. The existing plots are retained.

improvement.justification: v2 described the conservative alternative's potential width disadvantage without testing it. Figure 6 makes that practical tradeoff concrete, while clearer exposition and prior-work distinctions improve accessibility. These are limited gains because the core theory and existing experimental evidence remain unchanged.
